Tuned Mercedes-AMG G 63 Will Instantly Tell People You're Loaded. Do You Like the (Larte) Design?
17 photos
Photo: Instagram | lartedesign
After taking on various different rides recently, including a few Mercedes-AMG G 63s , Larte Design continues its tuning frenzy with yet another take on the popular German premium super truck.
The project is simply called the Mercedes-AMG G 63 by Larte Design, and the visual updates are said to fit the 2025 to 2025 model year cars. The styling part is more than visible, and will immediately tell bystanders that they are looking at a very special G-Wagen, regardless of whether they have a petrolhead license in their wallet or not, as the add-ons are definitely in-your-face.
Starting at the front, we can see that the bumper has been altered during the tuning process. This modded Mercedes-AMG G 63 has new air vent trim, and a quite fat apron. The latter looks more like a diffuser than a splitter due to its multi-fin design, though, but it is not on the brash side of things. Or is it? Actually, that is for you to decide, yet before inviting you to leave your impression on this project, we also have to go through other details that make it more special.
For instance, the grille is also on the special side of things, as it sports a new pattern that combines both horizontal and vertical slats, in a design that looks like a mix between a Benz and an AMG. Larte Design’s logo hasn’t replaced the three-pointed star emblem in the middle of the new grille, and we (or I in this case) think that that is a win. The turn signals have been smoked, and they flank the new hood that sports a more aggressive design, and has a pair of nostrils at the front.
Photo: Instagram | lartedesign Further back, this tuned Mercedes-AMG G 63 is home to a roof attachment above the front windscreen, which holds a pair of light strips on each side. It looks like this machine also features power running boards for easier ingress and egress. The rear bumper looks like the stock element to us, but the diffuser attached to it is anything but OEM. It features extra brake lights on the sides, and seems to have a cutout in the middle for the tow hook.
The custom spare wheel holder attached to the rear door is also part of the makeover, and it features a different pattern, and has Larte Design’s logo on it. Usually, the side-exit tailpipes of the Mercedes-AMG G 63 also get modded whenever most tuners get their hands on this model, but in this case, we are not sure that they have. The wheels, however, are entirely new, and seem to be about as big as the standard ones.
Finished in brushed silver, they provide some contrast to the rest of the exterior, which features a satin green look that is likely a wrap. The body kit add-ons were crafted of carbon fiber, and some of them, like the hood for instance, have a dry carbon look that contributes to the tuned Mercedes-AMG G 63’s more special nature.
The interior hasn’t been detailed in the pictures that Larte Design shared on its social media channels, and that’s because this project is all about the visual upgrades on the outside. However,zooming in through the windows in certain images reveals that black is the color that dominates the cockpit.
Photo: Instagram | lartedesign Do you know what the tuner hasn’t mentioned? That’s right, the powertrain. And this obviously tells us that the oily bits haven’t been touched with the tuning stick. As a result, this Mercedes-AMG G 63 should still have 577 hp (430 kW/585 ps) and 627 lb-ft (850 Nm) of torque to play with. Unless it actually boasts more oomph, which we doubt.
The 4.0-liter twin-turbocharged V8 engine allows the standard G 63 to hit 62 mph (100 kph) in 4.3 seconds from rest. The model has a top speed of up to 149 mph (240 kph), though in order to reach it, your modern-day AMG G-Wagen must have the optional AMG Driver’s Pack. Otherwise, the maximum speed will drop to 137 mph (220 kph), and that’s still more than enough for daily drives.
Larte Design hasn’t said anything about the pricing of this body kit at the time of writing, so if you want to find out how much it will cost you to make your new-age Mercedes-AMG G 63 looks like this, then you will have to reach out to the tuner directly. And if you do, feel free to tell us what the magical number is. By the way, don’t forget that these dry carbon elements are said to fit the 2025 to 2027 model year G 63.
Now, if you had such a thing and wanted to make it stand out more, would you actually opt for Larte Design’s bundle detailed above? I’d probably have second thoughts about it. View this post on Instagram A post shared by LARTE DESIGN | BODY KITS | WHEELS | AUTO DESIGN (@lartedesign)

How Much Does a 2017 Audi R8 Cost After 53,000 Miles?
12 photos
Photo: Instagram | motorcarsofchicago
Audi pulled the plug on the R8 two years ago, but that does not make it any less exciting, as we are still looking at a German supercar with Italian influences.
That’s because it may have been assembled at the Heilbronn facility in Germany by the four-ring brand, but beneath the skin lies the same platform as the Lamborghini Huracan. The Raging Bull’s previous-generation baby supercar was dropped for good in 2024, being replaced with the Temerario, and the R8 followed in its footsteps, as the assembly ceased in 2024 as well, after a ten-year production run.
During this time, the second-generation Audi R8 was offered as a two-door coupe and a two-door convertible (Spyder) featuring rear-wheel drive on certain models, and all-wheel drive on others. All of them had a longitudinal mid-engine layout, and packed the same mill as the Huracan. And that’s a 5.2-liter naturally aspirated V10, in case you forgot, which was good for 533 horsepower (540 ps/397 kW) in the base model.
Bring the V10 Plus variant into discussion, and the output will increase to 602 hp (610 ps/449 kW), and the thrust to 413 pound-feet (560 Nm), unlike the entry-level variant that offered 398 lb-ft (540 Nm) of torque originally. The lineup also comprises the R8 V10 RWS and R8 V10 Spyder RWS, with 533 hp (540 ps/397 kW) and 398 lb-ft (540 Nm) of torque, and the Spyder body style was also offered on other flavors of the supercar.
Photo: Instagram | motorcarsofchicago Even the slowest version of the second-generation Audi R8 took a couple of tenths of a second below the 4-second mark to reach 62 mph (100 kph) from a standstill, whereas the quickest did it in a little over three seconds. The top speed varied from one version to the other and from one body style to the other, and it ranged between 197 and 205 mph (317-330 kph).
The facelifted iteration was even faster, and the R8 V10 Performance Quattro, which was offered as a Coupe and Spyder, had 612 horsepower (620 ps/456 kW) and 428 pound-feet (580 Nm) of torque to play with, dropping the sprint time to 3.1 seconds, and increasing the maximum speed to 206 mph (331 kph) for the Coupe, and 3.2 seconds and 204 mph (329 kph) for the Spyder.
Audi’s second-generation R8 was briefly joined by the e-tron , which was introduced at the 2015 Geneva Motor Show. This was a battery-electric model with 456 horsepower in total from its pair of motors, four seconds required to zip to 62 mph, and a 280-mile (450 km) range promised by the four-ring brand. Thus, the company had an electric supercar before it was cool.
Now, we have talked about the second-gen Audi R8 as a whole a bit too much, so we should finally put the spotlight on the example pictured in the gallery, which is the whole reason behind this story. It is a 2027 model year supercar, as mentioned in the title, and as you can see, it features a blue paint finish on the outside, has the usual black details, rides on black wheels that spin around the gray brake calipers, and also sports tinted windows.
Photo: Instagram | motorcarsofchicago While the exterior is definitely sporty and quite exotic , the cockpit is on the gentleman side of things due to the use of brown leather upholstery on the seats, on the center console, and on parts of the door cards. The seats have diamond quilting on them, the pillars, headliner, and other parts of the interior were wrapped in black Alcantara, and we can also see some carbon fiber trim, a few metallic accents, and other bits and bobs.
This 2017 Audi R8 is said to have some 53,000 miles (85,300 km) on the clock, which makes it a high mileage supercar, though for what it’s worth, it looks very good for a blue-blooded exotic that has seen so much action over the years. There is a bit of wear on the driver’s seat outer bolsters, yet other than that, we do not see other flaws.
A 2017 model year Audi R8 usually ranges between $120,000 and upward of $170,000 for the V10 Plus Coupe, and if you want to spruce up your life with something like this, then you should not forget that its high maintenance could easily bankrupt you. After all, we are still talking about a supercar, and one that shares its DNA with a defunct Lambo.
But how much do you think one must cough out if they want to write their name on the dotted line in the papers of the pictured Audi R8? That would be $159,995, which was the asking price at the time of writing. We found this R8 on social media advertised by @motorcarsofchicago, and it is up to you to decide whether or not it’s worth that kind of money. This 20-Foot Tiny Home on Wheels Has Everything Two People Need and a Price Tag Under $50K
20 photos
Photo: Magic Box Tiny House
Over the last few decades, tiny homes have become an appealing housing option for people looking for a simplified lifestyle and lower living costs. But their appeal goes beyond private homeownership. Tiny houses have found a place in the travel and tourism industry as well, with many owners using compact models as Airbnb rentals and vacation retreats to offer guests the chance to experience what living small and more intentionally feels like.
A tiny house model that exemplifies this versatility and can fit both purposes is the Magic-Nordic from Magic Box Tiny House. Compact but comfortable and well-equipped, this tiny home on wheels can be either a haven for minimalist living or a lucrative Airbnb investment.
It features a practical layout with room for a sofa, a complete kitchen, a private bathroom, and a queen-size sleeping loft, covering the essentials for full-time living without adding overly complicated features.
The Magic-Nordic tiny house is built on a dual-axle trailer and has a length of 20 feet (6 meters). Its width is 8.2 feet (2.5 meters) and it stands 13 feet (4.1 meters) tall, which means it can be legally towed on public roads. This should make it an appealing option for those who like to travel with their home in tow or plan on moving frequently.
On the outside, it looks just like what most people picture when thinking of a tiny house on wheels . A pitched roof, a combination of metal and stained cedar siding, large windows, and a black metal roof give it the look of a conventional tiny home.
Photo: Magic Box Tiny House A glass door leads inside, where you discover a luminous living space that is well configured and beautifully styled, in perfect harmony with the elegant exterior. While many tiny house interiors are finished in classic bright white, Magic Nordic embraces a warmer color palette, but the minimalistic design and ample glazing keep it luminous and airy.
There is the glass entry door, plus a couple of large windows in the living room and several transom windows that let lots of natural light flood the interior, while the gabled roofline draws the eye upward and creates generous headroom in the sleeping loft.
The Magic-Nordic offers a footprint of just 180 square feet (16.7 square meters), including the loft, but it’s enough for all the essentials. The layout is simple and intuitive, with an open-plan ground floor that comprises the kitchen, living area, and the private bathroom, and a mezzanine dedicated to sleeping.
Photo: Magic Box Tiny House As in many tiny homes, the kitchen is the heart of the house. It’s compact but fully functional, with low and upper cabinets for storage, a sink with a cover, a gas oven and a four-burner cooktop. There is enough counter space to place other plug-in appliances, as well as dedicated space for future additions, such as a small under-bench fridge or a washer/dryer unit.
In terms of styling, the kitchen boasts black cabinets contrasted by white solid surface countertops, which give it an elegant, modern look. For dining, there is a separate bar table with high bar stools between the kitchen and living room.
There is room for a full-size sofa in the lounge area, and two large windows in this area of the house open it to the outside world. Located under the loft, the ceiling is a bit lower than in the kitchen, but the windows compensate with more openness.
Photo: Magic Box Tiny House The home’s loft bedroom is particularly interesting because it offers generous headroom and is fitted with multiple windows. Moreover, it accommodates a queen-size mattress and has a protection wall that doubles as storage space. The staircase that leads up to it also incorporates plenty of storage cubbies, something that prospective owners planning to use the house long-term will appreciate.
The private bathroom is another important aspect for full-time occupancy. Hidden behind a barn door, it comes with a shower, a toilet, and a small vanity with a ceramic sink, while a water heater provides hot water. The house also includes washer and dryer hookups.
The minimalist design and understated style blend seamlessly with modern amenities, including a Tuya smart living system, discrete lighting, and a 9,000-BTU mini-split air conditioning and heating system.
Photo: Magic Box Tiny House The house is built on a steel frame, which makes the structure durable, and the manufacturer offers this model with larger dimensions as well, from 24 to 40 feet (7.3 to 12.2 meters) in length. It’s ANSI A119.5-certified and DOT-approved, and customization options are also available, including exterior colors, window placement, and interior layout and finishes.
Magic Box is a China-based builder that ships its tiny houses from its factory in China to markets including the United States, Australia, and Canada. On its website, the company advertises prices up to 40% lower than locally built models. The Magic-Nordic, for instance, has a starting price of just $45,000, although the final cost will depend on the chosen configuration, shipping, and applicable import charges.

Private Mopar Collection Hides 1968 Hemi GTX Ragtop 1-of-1, Owner Turned Down a Superbird for It
15 photos
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150
Some people just win the lottery. Others develops sophisticated schemes and systems designed to improve the odds and up the chances at a get-rich-fast’n’easy jackpot, some just walk in, pick a random ticket, and become millionaires. That’s about the same statistical randomness that made an Oregon Moparhead strike the deal of a lifetime several times in a row. This time, it’s a Hemi GTX ragtop.
Rarely does a collector car combine one-of-a-kind factory provenance with a lighting-strikes-thrice mechanical reunion across 3,000 miles of United States of Automobile. Well, prepare for yet another unbelievable story from the Mopar history treasure trove of Gary Myers' workshop in Vernonia, Oregon.
The man is probably the coolest Mopar collector anywhere, and not necessarily for his cars (although he does own a special gathering of holy grails), but also for the stories that come with each and every one of those. I’m telling you right here, in writing, the man is a great candidate for case studies on how does luck work. Of course, someone would have to quantify luck in the restrained, limited confinements of science before such a venture would be practicable, but we digress.
Troy Bergeron, the larger-than-life gearhead and Moparhead from Mopars5150 YouTube channel came face-to-face with a 1968 Plymouth Hemi GTX convertible finished in deep GG1 Forest Green metallic over a white interior, white top, and white stripes. And that’s just the beginning of the options list. In fact, it’s far easier to say what didn’t come on it, because it’s just one add-on – the black-out hood treatment. Everything else was put on it.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 You must be wondering who’d buy a Hemi Mopar loaded with everything, and for what. To show off is the answer to the “why,” but this car wasn’t ordered by a private client with a knack for high-horse cheap B-body ChryCo automobiles. I know, the GTX was the top dog in the Plymouth lineup of intermediates during its tenure (1967-1971), but it was still a product of the lowest-cost division in the Chrysler Motors Corporation hierarchy.
Plymouth introduced the GTX as a special trim on the Belvedere in 1967 as the "Gentleman's Muscle Car," pairing upscale interior appointments and distinctive styling with standard big-block power. If that sounds even remotely familiar, let me remind you of the road runner. No, not the Road Runner from 1968, but the one from 1967. The one Dodge introduced. Yes, Dodge. You know, the Coronet R/T? The Fratzog boys dubbed it “the road runner.”
Plymouth countered with the GTX package on its run-of-the-mill mid-sizer, the trusty Belvedere. Produced as a standalone model from 1968 through 1971—before transitioning into an optional performance package on the Road Runner between 1972 and 1974—the GTX received Chrysler's sleekly contoured second-generation B-body architecture for the 1968 model year, resulting in 18,940 total units built.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 The model year was the all-time highwater mark for the moniker, which had the misfortune of being in the same division, at the same time, in the same place with the lowest-buck, highest-bang Mopar of them all – the Plymouth Road Runner.
Of those 18,940 examples assembled for 1968, 17,914 were two-door hardtops and only 1,026 were two-door convertibles. While the vast majority carried the standard 375-hp (380-PS) 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) Super Commando V8, a mere 446 buyers checked the box for the 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) Hemi V8 rated at 425 hp (431 PS) and 490 lb-ft (664 Nm) of torque. Only 36 of those 1968 Hemi GTXs were convertibles.
Within that microscopic run of 36 Hemi drop-tops built for the United States market, just 24 were equipped with the heavy-duty A727 TorqueFlite 3-speed automatic transmission, while 12 received the 4-speed manual. According to Mopar historian Galen Govier, who personally inspected and decoded Gary's convertible, only a dozen examples were previously known to exist in the registry, alongside two additional survivors Gary knows of in Canada, bringing the surviving total to 14.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 Even among those 14 remaining relics, Gary's car stands alone as a documented 1-of-1 configuration. Built as Chrysler's West Coast Public Relations vehicle for 1968, it is one of the two green 1968 Hemi GTX convertibles ever produced, and the only one paired with a white interior. Because PR fleet cars were loaded to showcase the catalog, it carries every single factory option except the hood blackout paint. I assume it wouldn’t have made much of a visual impact to put black next to dark green?
That exhaustive option sheet even includes a bizarre factory three-passenger rear seatbelt option across a convertible rear bench that measures barely 4 feet (1.2 meters) wide. Of course, safety wasn’t the end-of-worlds topic that has grown into today, but it was still nice to show prospects that the division cared for the occasional back seat occupants.
To ensure the cabin remained period-perfect, Gary spent $1,000 for a mint original woodgrain steering wheel pulled from a vintage driving simulator and paid $440 at the Mopars at the Strip show in Las Vegas for an uncracked original green center console.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 When Gary first acquired the convertible—having walked away from a $7,000 deal on a disassembled Sublime 1970 Superbird in central Oregon so he could afford the GTX—the car lacked its original engine and transmission. Some would say that’s unlucky, but Gary is not accustomed to that notion. Not by a long mile.
He tracked down a properly-coded 1968 Hemi block out of a Dodge Coronet, and then spotted an East Coast magazine advertisement from an elderly transmission builder selling a genuine 1968 Hemi TorqueFlite unit for $1,200.
The seller explained that a drag racer had brought a brand-new 1968 Hemi B-body into his shop back in 1968 to swap in a manual-valve-body race transmission, leaving the factory automatic untouched under the shop workbench for over more than three decades. After making Gary promise to tear it apart and inspect the internals before running it, the seller accepted a $400 deposit and had a friend crate the transmission for air freight.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 Shipped across the continent to Portland via Forward Air, the transmission arrived at Gary's shop, where a glance at the stamped serial pad nearly knocked him off his feet. The vehicle identification number stamped into the transmission case was one single digit ahead of his GTX's VIN.
Against astronomical odds, an East Coast transmission sitting under a bench since 1968 had come from the Hemi car built immediately ahead of his West Coast convertible PR showboater. Care to debate luck now?
When Gary opened the transmission pump as promised, the factory BorgWarner ink stamps were still freshly visible across the clutch packs. That’s how new the original, numbers-matching car was – most probably, the one who ditched it didn’t even drive his car.
Delighted by the miracle and amused that the seller's crate builder had warned the old man about how Gary would scam him, our Oregon Moparhead mailed a final check with an extra $100 enclosed, instructing the seller to take his skeptical friend out to lunch and tell him that was how West Coast car guys kept their word. Pay it forward? Attracting abundance? I prefer “righteous man,” and everything good in Gary’s life is definitely well deserved.

2026 SEMA Show • 2027 Toyota Crown Signia Gets GT-S Concept Treatment for SEMA, Becomes a Sleek Wagon
Holy Grail 1968 Shelby GT500 4-Speed Rocks Two Cool Factory Option, Pick Your Favorite Arm and Leg
30 photos
Photo: Mecum
Late in the 1960s, the American pony car war stopped being a polite neighborhood rivalry and turned into an all-out arms race. Carroll Shelby had already conquered road courses with his nimble small-block fastbacks, yet buyers were demanding thunderous big-block torque paired with grand touring refinement. Whenever an authentic representative from that brief transitional era surfaces with bulletproof factory documentation, serious collectors prepare for a fierce, high-stakes auction room battle.
That exact scenario played out on October 24, 2026, when a stunning 1968 Shelby GT500 Fastback rolled onto the stage at the Mecum Dallas-Fort Worth auction as Lot S190. Documented in a recent feature on the CARFINDER YouTube channel, the classic muscle car hammered sold for $297,000. Only weeks earlier, the same machine had been listed by Kinion Auto Sales and Service in Clarence, Iowa, displaying 80,170 miles (129,021 km).
By the time the fastback reached the Texas block, its odometer read 80,179 miles (129,036 km), adding nine transit miles to a storied six-decade life. Identified by Ford VIN 8T02S130891 and Shelby serial number 00800, this car was assembled at the Metuchen, New Jersey, plant on December 14, 1967. Per official Shelby Registry records, the car was delivered to Levittown Motors in Levittown, New York.
Sold new on Long Island on June 15, 1968, serial number #00800 stood out thanks to an uncommon factory color combination. While most buyers chose black cabins, this example paired Candyapple Red paint and white side stripes with Saddle Decor bucket seats. Its Elite Marti Report confirms that out of 92 Candyapple Red four-speed GT500 fastbacks built, only seventeen received Saddle upholstery, and just one went to Levittown Motors.
Photo: Mecum Benefiting from a meticulous restoration, this GT500 is loaded with desirable factory equipment. Alongside its 4-speed manual gearbox and 3.50:1 rear axle, the build sheet includes factory air conditioning (cool #1), the Extra Cooling Package (cool #2), power steering, and power front disc brakes.
Cabin and exterior highlights encompass a Swing-Away steering column, the Sport Deck fold-down rear seat, shoulder harnesses, the Visibility Group, bright wheel lip moldings, and original 10-spoke cast-aluminum Shelby wheels.
That long list of creature comforts reflected a major philosophical shift for the marque in 1968, when Ford officially rebranded the lineup under the Shelby Cobra moniker. Because Shelby American and Ford were starting to build a wall around each other’s friend-zone outer limits, Ford Motor Company shipped unfinished Metuchen Mustangs by rail to A.O. Smith Corporation in Ionia, Michigan.
Workers there installed fiberglass front clips, twin-scoop hoods, side brake ducts, integral roll bars, and sequential Mercury Cougar taillights.
Photo: Mecum Despite 1968 marking the highest single-year volume in vintage Shelby history, Kevin Marti’s official factory records show how scarce each configuration remains across all 4,451 total units built. The GT350, powered by a J-code 302-cubic-inch (4.9-liter) V8 rated at 250 hp (253 PS), accounted for 1,457 cars. Truth be told, that was a major step back for the moniker, which had lost 56 hp in one blow, while also putting on 17 extra cubic inches.
That tally comprises 1,053 fastbacks, including 821 four-speed manuals and 232 three-speed automatics, alongside 404 convertibles, divided into 177 four-speeds and 227 automatics.
Big-block production began with the S-code GT500, which totaled 1,423 examples: one notchback coupe prototype, 1,020 fastbacks, and 402 convertibles. Only 405 GT500 fastbacks received the four-speed manual gearbox alongside 615 automatics, while convertibles split into 153 four-speeds and 249 automatics.
Photo: Mecum Mid-year, the R-code 428 Cobra Jet birthed the GT500KR, totaling 1,571 cars: 1,053 fastbacks, with 530 four-speeds and 523 automatics, plus 518 convertibles, with 267 four-speeds and 251 automatics.
Underneath the fiberglass hood of early-1968 GT500s like serial number 00800 beats the S-code 428-cubic-inch (seven liters) V8. Not to be confused with the equally-displacing Cobra Jet launched mid-year in 1968, this is the fabled Police Interceptor. Debuting for the 1966 model year in Ford’s FE big-block family, the Police Interceptor remained in law enforcement catalog production until 1970, although Shelby retired it at the end of the 1968 production run.
Built for sustained high-speed durability rather than NHRA homologation, the 428 Police Interceptor featured a 4.13-inch (104.9-mm) bore, a 3.98-inch (101.1-mm) stroke, and 10.5:1 compression ratio. Whereas the 1967 GT500 used dual four-barrel carburetors rated at 355 hp (360 PS), the 1968 GT500 adopted a single 715-cfm Holley carburetor on an aluminum Cobra intake, producing 360 hp (365 PS) at 5,400 rpm and 420 lb-ft (569 Nm) at 3,200 rpm.
Photo: Mecum While the subsequent 428 Cobra Jet gained larger-valve heads, heavy-duty connecting rods, and functional ram-air induction under a sandbagged 335-hp (340-PS) and 440-lb-ft (597-Nm) rating, the 428 Police Interceptor was no slouch in period tests. Car buffs magazines pushed a 4-speed 428 Police Interceptor GT500 from 0 to 60 mph (97 kph) in 6.5 seconds, running the quarter-mile in 14.5 seconds at 99 mph (159 kph) toward a 132-mph (212-kph) top speed.
Outside the Shelby stable, the P-code 428 Police Interceptor earned its stripes powering full-size state trooper pursuit sedans, including the Ford Custom, Custom 500, and Galaxie 500, plus Mercury’s Monterey, Montclair, Park Lane, and Marauder cruisers.
Its Q-code civilian sibling also motivated the Ford Thunderbird and Ford Galaxie 500 7-Litre, the 1966-only full-sizer that wasn’t afraid to take on any intermediate from across Detroit, or the equally nefarious big showboaters with muscle-bound big-inchers (thing Catalina 2+2, Impala 427, Buick Wildcat GS – you get the idea). Bearing that relentless highway-interdiction pedigree, Candyapple Red Shelby number 00800 easily justified every penny of its $297,000 Texas hammer price.

This Handcrafted Transit Camper Van Was Built by a Veteran Carpenter, It's Now for Sale
26 photos
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / brianmcgaha
Today's featured project is based on a 2026 AWD Ford Transit 350 with a 148" wheelbase and a high roof, finished in a rare Wild Green paint.
It was created by Pinnacle Campers, a Boise, Idaho-based company specializing in custom camper vans. Brian McGaha founded the company in reaction to a growing amount of clients requesting camper van conversions and vehicle upfitting. He has been a carpenter and a residential remodeling contractor for around 30 years.
As always, let's first take a look at the van's exterior. The vehicle rides on VanCentric wheels wrapped in Falken Wildpeak all-terrain tires.
The van came with a Quigley Q-Lift paired with a Bilstein strut and shock upgrade – they offer a 2-inch lift and better stability when driving both on and off the beaten path.
At the rear, you'll come across a setup I haven't seen before. There's an FVC (Flatline Van Co.) spare tire carrier/ladder combo attached to the driver-side door - that's a super common upgrade . However, the part that I haven't seen before is an A/C unit mounted to it.
Climb on top of the van, and you'll discover an AVC RIG roof rack holding a 600 W solar array and a flat-mounted Starlink antenna.
Other notable mods are Transit Trail running boards, power and water hookups, a CR Laurence window on the driver's side, and flares.
Flares, also known as pods or capsules, are designed to increase the van width to allow you to fit a bed in an east to west arrangement instead of the standard north to south. This rig's Flarespace flares are paint matched to the van's color.
The rugged exterior theme shifts to a more modern, homey look inside the van. The interior has an open layout, with no wall separating the driver's cabin from the living space. However, you can use a large curtain to separate the two areas for more privacy.
Regarding aesthetics, you'll notice Lonseal Madera "mushroom" flooring, custom white cabinetry with a two-part epoxy finish, brown automotive tweed fabric on the walls, and a grey ceiling with 8 lights. The look is complemented by a stained walnut countertop.
The first part of the living space is a seating area located dead ahead as you enter. It comprises a large bench with a Lagun table mount and several storage compartments.
The bench also hides an unexpected feature: a shower. Specifically, if you lift one of the bench's tops, you'll reveal a stainless steel shower pan and showerhead connected to a mixer. To complete the shower setup, you must hang a curtain to hooks on the ceiling. It's a really small setup, but it will do the job whenever you don't have access to a public shower.
Next, we have the kitchen on the passenger side. It features a stainless steel sink with a fold-down faucet and a small cover, a slide-out housing a portable single-burner 1,800 W induction cooktop (that can also be accessed from outside the van), and another slide-out holding a 45-liter Dometic CFX345 chest-style fridge.
An overhead cabinet, two drawers, and a lower cabinet are available for storage in the kitchen. Moreover, on the opposite side, you'll come across a relatively tall unit integrating a drawer and three open storage compartments.
Two of the storage compartments hold bins, and the third and largest one at the bottom has a Trelino separating toilet.
Beside the kitchen overhead cabinet, Brian devised a simple control panel for some of the rig's utilities. It has a monitor for the water tank, a thermostat, and light switches (including a main dimmer switch) and switches for the inverter, Starlink system, and water pump.
Finally, you'll discover a fixed bed arrangement in the back part of the living space. It's 75 inches (190 centimeters) long and 52 inches (132 centimeters) wide, with a 6-inch-thick (15-centimeter-thick) memory foam mattress. The bedroom also offers four overhead cabinets (two on each side) and two reading lights.
You can store your largest items in the garage underneath the bedroom, which is accessible from both inside and outside the van. Besides offering room for cargo in its middle part, the garage has two boxes on the sides that offer extra storage space and accommodate part of the utility systems.
Power is on the left side – the electrical system's highlights are two 300 Ah lithium batteries and a 2,500 W inverter. Three charging sources help keep the batteries topped off: solar power, shore power, and DC-DC charging while the engine is running thanks to two 50-amp DC-DC chargers.
As for plumbing, the van is equipped with a 21-gallon (79-liter) freshwater tank, a heated and under-mounted 16-gallon (60-liter) greywater tank, a Seaflo pump with an accumulator, an Aqua Crest water filter, and an outdoor shower connection.
The last important system is an Elwell Timberline hydronic heater providing both heated air and hot water. On those hot days, the Nomadic Cooling S1 mounted at the back of the van can rapidly cool you off, as its internal unit sits right next to the bed.
All in all, Brian created a mobile home with the right blend of practicality, comfort, and storage space. As mentioned in the title, this Transit-based camper is now for sale.
According to Pinnacle Campers' listing , its price tag is $154,500 (€138,617). Considering the fact that it's a brand-new platform with less than 900 miles (1,448 km) and all of the comforts it offers, that's a fair price.

Mansory-Tuned Audi RS6 Avant Is a Supercar Posing as a Spacious Wagon
18 photos
Photo: Instagram | _kourosh_mansory
While Audi is fine-tuning the upcoming RS 6 family , which will comprise not only the Avant (station wagon) body style but also the Sedan, in a premiere since the C6-generation made from 2007 to 2011, the defunct C8 RS 6 Avant keeps making headlines.
It feels like every tuner that matters and their pet have decided to homage this model before its successor arrives, as we have seen numerous modified examples these past few weeks and months. One of the latest to have crossed our screens is the Mansory-modded machine pictured above in the gallery, which truly is something else.
Yeah, I know how Mansory tends to roll, by bringing out the brashness within its projects more often than not. However, in this case, the controversial tuner has really outdone itself. That’s because the Audi RS 6 Avant in question truly is a head-turning machine, both inside and out, and if that weren’t enough, then you should also know that it boasts more power than the original Bugatti Veyron. You know, the world’s first hypercar.
Starting on the outside, we can see that this ride features plenty of add-ons at the front, including a fat splitter, grille surrounds, and flaps on the sides of the bumper. The hood is also new, from what we can tell, and so are the door mirror casings. The side skirts, roof-mounted wing, tailgate spoiler, and rear diffuser have also come from the quoted tuner’s portfolio, just like the 22-inch wheels, which are called the FD.15.
Photo: Instagram | _kourosh_mansory Some of the add-ons have a carbon finish, others are presented in blue, and the car’s overall look is glossy black. And since black tends to hide most brash tuning jobs perfectly, it is probably why I think that this modded Audi RS 6 Avant is on the very cool side of things. I’d also want to see it dressed in a more vibrant exterior color, as chances are I might think it is quite kitschy.
Such builds often have a mix of leather and Alcantara on the inside, as well as some extra carbon fiber trim, among other things. However, in this case, Mansory dressed the pictured car with tartan upholstery on the seats, door cards, and central armrest. Other components have been wrapped in black leather, and we can also see some blue stitching.
The illuminated tread plates greet users upon opening the doors, and other highlights include the numerous Mansory emblems, the special floor mats with diamond quilting and blue outer edges, the illuminated logos on the seatbacks, the new carbon-like trim, partially wrapped Alcantara steering wheel, more Alcantara upholstery on the door armrests, blue seatbelts with Mansory’s name on them, and a few other things.
As you likely know, the Audi RS 6 Avant from this generation has 621 hp (630 ps/463 kW) and 627 lb-ft (850 Nm) of torque from its 4.0-liter twin-turbocharged V8 engine. The model hits 62 mph (100 kph) in just a little over three seconds, and has a top speed electronically capped at 155 mph (250 kph). Therefore, it is already faster than some previous-generation supercars.
However, the Mansory-tuned example pictured in the gallery has even more oomph on tap, as the tuner says that the car’s output has increased to a whopping 1,085 hp (1,100 ps/ 809 kW) and 922 pound-feet (1,250 Nm) of torque. We cannot tell you how fast this ride is, as Mansory hasn’t released these numbers at the time of writing. However, the 0-62 mph sprint time has likely entered the 2-second realm.
Photo: Instagram | _kourosh_mansory Thus, all we can say before rounding off the story and moving on to the next one is “Congrats, Mansory!” This tuner certainly knows how to positively surprise us after all these years, and we hope we will see more cool projects from the in the near future.
Now, before proceeding to the next story, we will remind you that the new-gen Audi RS 6 is right around the corner, and, as mentioned above, it will launch in two body styles. The Sedan will join the Avant after a long wait, and rumor has it that the two might feature an electrified twin-turbocharged V6 engine with plug-in hybrid capabilities, which is understood to churn out around 740 hp (750 ps/552 kW) in total.
If that number is correct, then it will be punchier than the BMW M5, which is its biggest rival in the class. The latter has a PHEV 4.4-liter twin-turbo V8 making 717 hp (727 ps/535 kW), and while the sedan requires 3.4 seconds from 0-60 mph (0-97 kph), the Touring (station wagon) completes the sprint in 3.5 seconds.
Both the Sedan and Avant versions of the next-gen Audi RS 6 will end up in our market, and chances are that they might reach dealers nationwide either for the 2027 or maybe the 2028 model year. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Kourosh Mansory (@_kourosh_mansory)
